paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea: you can bring the LORD the very bottom of your life, and He hears it. The writer cries "Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!" (Psalm 130:1). He doesn't clean himself up first or show up with a list of good deeds. He asks for mercy, because he knows "If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?" (Psalm 130:3).

But then comes the turn, and it's the best part. "But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared" (Psalm 130:4). So the writer waits, and he puts his hope in the LORD's word, because "with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance" (Psalm 130:5, 7). That's why waiting doesn't have to be hopeless, friend. Your hope rests on who the LORD is, and that never moves.

Then David shows what that hope looks like on the inside: a soul stilled and quieted, "like a weaned child with his mother" (Psalm 131:2). He isn't chasing great things or matters too lofty for him (Psalm 131:1). I think that's the peace of someone who stopped trying to carry it all. Both songs end with the same call: "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD…" (Psalm 130:7; 131:3), and that call is for you today, baker, from the depths all the way to quiet rest.
